title: Supramolecular delivery of senolytics enables targeted anti-senescence therapy and accelerated fracture healing

sections.abstract:
Current clinical management of fractures relies largely on surgical intervention and systemic pharmacotherapy, both of which are frequently associated with side effects and largely neglect early microenvironmental abnormalities. Precise elimination of senescent cells at the early stage may offer a more efficient means of restoring microenvironmental homeostasis and resetting regenerative dynamics. To this end, we designed and synthesized a multifunctional supramolecular nanoplatform, Asp 10 SAC4A, based on combination of host–guest recognition and self-assembly to simultaneously address three fundamental challenges in selectively eliminating senescent cells at the fracture site: inadequate targeting, insufficient responsiveness, and poor coordination of multi-drug delivery. The platform consists of an azocalix [ 4 ]arene modified with a deca-aspartate (Asp 10 ) peptide for selective binding to newly exposed hydroxyapatite at fracture sites, enabling active localization. Simultaneously, Dasatinib and Quercetin are co-loaded in a controlled ratio, and triggered for rapid release through the hypoxia-responsive mechanism of the azo groups, achieving microenvironment-specific “source-clearing” therapy. This strategy significantly alleviates inflammation, enhances osteogenesis and accelerates fracture healing. These results highlight the crucial role of selectively targeting senescent cells in the early phase of fracture and offer an innovative therapeutic approach that improves treatment efficiency and prognosis. Overall, this study aims to establish a fracture-site–activated senolytic delivery strategy that integrates fracture targeting, hypoxia-triggered release, and combination therapy, thereby enabling precise early-stage anti-senescence intervention to accelerate fracture healing.

sections.introduction:
Fractures are one of the most common and burdensome organ injuries globally [ 1 ], with approximately 178 million new cases in 2019 [ 2 ]. The annual direct medical costs associated with fractures have exceeded $25 billion in the U.S. alone, a burden that is projected to increase further as the population ages [ 3 , 4 ]. Despite advances in surgical and pharmacologic treatments, delayed fracture healing and fracture non-union are still prevalent, especially in older patients [ 5 ]. Currently, the treatment of fracture mainly relies on surgical interventions (e.g., internal fixation or bone grafting) and systemic medications (e.g., osteoinductive agents). However, surgical treatments have limitations such as high invasiveness, increased risk of infection, and frequent postoperative complications, which are particularly challenging in patients with comorbidities [ 6 ]. Systemic medications, such as bisphosphonates or osteoanabolic hormones, can cause serious side effects [ 7 , 8 ]; topical applications are also susceptible to off-target drug diffusion, which can lead to ectopic ossification [ 9 ]. More importantly, these traditional treatments are mainly used in the middle and late stages of fracture healing and have limited effect on the regulation of the local tissue microenvironment in the early stage [ 10 ], which determines the speed and quality of healing [ 11 ]. Therefore, how to optimize the local microenvironment at the early stage of fracture to promote bone regeneration safely and efficiently has become a major challenge in the field of orthopedics.

Recent studies have shown that after fracture, senescent cells can be rapidly induced and accumulate in the injured area, and their continuous secretion of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors significantly aggravates the inflammatory response at the fracture site and hinders tissue regeneration and fracture healing [ 12 , 13 ]. It is noteworthy that this phenomenon is not only seen in aged individuals, but is also observed in young healthy individuals during fracture healing [ 14 ]. Therefore, targeted removal of senescent cells not only provides a new therapeutic target and strategy for fracture repair [ 15 ], but also provides an effective intervention pathway to improve the local microenvironment and accelerate tissue repair in the early stages of fracture [ 10 ]. However, no senescent cell removal therapy has yet been applied in the clinic because senescent cells also play an important role in physiological processes such as tissue remodeling and wound healing [ 16 ], and this inherent functional duality and opposing needs (i.e., removal of the harmful versus retention of the beneficial) constitute the central dilemma of current senescent cell removal strategies [ 17 , 18 ], which greatly limits the clinical application of senescent cell elimination strategies (senolytics) in fracture management [ 19 ]. Therefore, the core issue to be addressed is how to achieve multidimensional regulation in space, time and dose, so as to be able to dynamically coordinate the context-dependent biological effects of senescent cells in different tissues or physiopathological situations, and to achieve the precise inhibition of harmful functions and the maintenance of beneficial functions in the complex process of biological system regulation.

Addressing the above core problem requires facing several key challenges simultaneously. First, treatments must be specific to the fracture site rather than the intact bone tissue to avoid off-target toxicity, which limits the use of traditional systemic bone-targeting medicines such as bisphosphonates; second, alterations in the local microenvironment (e.g., hypoxia, pH changes, or inflammatory signals) need to be taken into account for intelligent and controlled drug release. Controlled release is essential for senolytic therapy due to the “hit-and-run” nature of senolytic agents [ 20 ], which require only brief exposure is sufficient to trigger apoptosis of senescent cells, without the need for continuous drug administration [ 20 , 21 ]; finally, in current senolytic strategies, the classic Dasatinib (D) and Quercetin (Q) combination has demonstrated superior therapeutic efficacy over monotherapy through complementary mechanisms [ 22 ]. The rationale for combining D and Q is that senescent cells rely on partially distinct senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways (SCAPs), and D and Q inhibit overlapping but non-identical pro-survival networks, thereby broadening senolytic coverage and enhancing efficacy [ 23 , 24 ]. However, achieving optimal synergistic effects requires precise spatiotemporal coordination of both agents at a controlled stoichiometric ratio. Overall, this multilayered, cross-disciplinary integration of design goals is exceptionally complex, and no mature platform has yet been able to fulfill all these requirements at the same time.

To address the aforementioned multiple challenges in achieving precise elimination of senescent cells in the fracture region, we developed a nanodelivery platform based on Asp 10 -modified azocalix [ 4 ]arene (Asp 10 SAC4A, Scheme 1 ). The platform design is inspired by the unique advantages of supramolecular systems in drug delivery. Macrocyclic hosts (e.g., cyclodextrins, calixarenes, cucurbiturils) were selected as the carrier framework due to their well-defined structures, explicit recognition sites, and thermodynamically controlled quantifiable/reproducible drug loading [ 25 ]. Azocalixarene was specifically chosen for its exceptional broad-spectrum drug loading capacity combined with hypoxia-responsive drug release capability at fracture sites [ 26 ]. Then, Asp 10 was chosen as a targeting moiety, leveraging its high affinity for newly exposed hydroxyapatite to achieve precise bone fracture site-specific targeting rather than systemic bone tissue. Ultimately, the modified Asp 10 SAC4A forms stable nanostructures via supramolecular self-assembly, integrating multiple macrocyclic cavities into single nanoparticle to thermodynamically enable ratio-controlled delivery of senolytic agents [ 27 ]. The supramolecular system achieved the co-loading of D and Q at predetermined ratios. A series of in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated therapeutic effects while elucidating underlying mechanisms of anti-senescence and microenvironment remodeling. These results fully demonstrate this design not only takes into account the three major needs of fracture targeting, local stimulation response and multidrug co-delivery, but also provides a new technological pathway for the development of safe and efficient therapeutic strategies for senescent cell clearance.

sections.methods:
All the reagents and solvents were commercially available and used as received unless otherwise specified purification. 4-Aminobenzoic acid, 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid, sodium acetate trihydrate and sodium nitrite were purchased from Aladdin. 1,1’,3,3,3’,3’-Hexamethylindodicarbocyanine (CY5-DM) was obtained OKeanos Tech. Co.,Ltd. Quercetin (Q), dasatinib (D), sodium dithionite (SDT) and tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride were purchased from Bidepharmatech. Ltd. The peptide SH‑Asp10 was purchased from Shanghai Jill Biochemical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Sulfonate azocalix [ 4 ]arenes was synthesized according to the previous literature [ 69 ].

1 H and 13 C NMR data were recorded on a Bruker AV400 spectrometer. Mass spectra were performed on an Agilent 6520 Q-TOF LC/MS (ESI). UV-Vis spectra were recorded in a quartz cell (light path 10 mm) on a Cary 100 UV-Vis spectrophotometer equipped with a Cary dual cell peltier accessory. Fluorescence measurements were recorded in a conventional quartz cell (light path 10 mm) on Cary Eclipse and PerkinElmer FL6500. The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) sample was examined by a TEM (HITACHI HT7800 Exalens). The sample solutions for dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements were examined on a laser light scattering spectrometer (NanoBrook 173plus and Brookhaven ZetaPals/BI-200SM). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Waters, Alliance2695, USA) was employed to perform chromatographic analysis.

MCAC4A was synthesized according to previously reported method [ 70 ]. In details, 4-aminobenzoic acid (411 mg, 3.00 mmol), concentrated hydrochloric acid (0.5 mL), and distilled water (10 mL) were first added to a 50 mL round-bottomed flask. After the mixture turning into a clear and colorless solution, it was cooled to 0–5 °C. Next, NaNO 2 (207 mg, 3.00 mmol) was dissolved in distilled water (5 mL) and added dropwise to the 50 mL round-bottomed flask at 0–5 °C to generate the diazonium salt. Subsequently, C4A (1.27 g, 3.00 mmol), sodium acetate trihydrate (1.22 g, 9.00 mmol), methanol (15 mL), and DMF (24 mL) were added sequentially to a 100 mL round-bottomed flask and cooled to 0–5 °C. The diazonium salt in the 50 mL round-bottomed flask was slowly added in a dropwise manner into the mixed solution containing C4A, while maintaining the temperature of the reaction system at 0–5 °C. The mixture was stirred for 2 h and then transferred to room temperature for another 2 h. The solvent was removed under vacuo, and the product was separated by column chromatography ( V : V , dichloromethane: methanol = 50:1) to obtain orange powder, MCAC4A.

CSAC4A was synthesized according to previously reported method [ 70 ]. In details, 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid (520 mg, 3.00 mmol), Na 2 CO 3 (155 mg, 1.50 mmol), and distilled water (5 mL) were added sequentially to a 25 mL round-bottomed flask. After 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid was fully dissolved, the mixed solution was cooled to 0–5 °C. Next, NaNO 2 (207 mg, 3 mmol) in distilled water (5 mL) was added slowly to the mixture containing 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid to generate the diazonium salt. Subsequently, 0.6 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid was added dropwise to this solution while maintaining the temperature at 0–5 °C. Meanwhile, MCAC4A (430 mg, 0.75 mmol), sodium acetate trihydrate (1.22 g, 9 mmol), methanol (15 mL), and DMF (24 mL) were added into another 100 mL round- bottomed flask and cooled to 0–5 °C. Then, the diazonium salt solution was added slowly in a dropwise-manner to solutions containing MCAC4A, with the temperature kept in the range of 0–5 °C. The mixture was stirred for 2 h and then transferred to room temperature for another 2 h. Afterword, 50 mL of dilute HCl was then added to the reaction solution, heated up to 60 °C, and kept for 30 min. The solvent was removed under vacuum. The residue was recrystallized with methanol and water to afford brick red CSAC4A.

Mal-SAC4A was synthesized according to previously reported method [ 71 ]. In details, CSAC4A (200 mg, 0.18 mmol) was dissolved in DMF (20 mL), followed by the addition of DIPEA (44 mg, 0.34 mmol) and HATU (78 mg, 0.21 mmol). After stirring at room temperature for 30 min, 1-[2-(2-Aminoethoxy) ethyl] pyrrole-2,5-dione (67 mg, 0.35 mmol) was added to the reaction system, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature for another 12 h. The solvent was removed under vacuum, and the residue was recrystallized with methanol and water to obtain brick red Mal-SAC4A.

The phosphate buffered saline (PBS) solution of pH = 7.4 was prepared by dissolving 0.603 g of sodium phosphate monobasic dehydrate, 0.870 g disodium phosphate, 8.01 g sodium chloride and 0.201 g potassium chloride in approximate 900 mL double-distilled water. Titrate to pH = 7.4 at the lab temperature of 25 °C with NaOH and make up volume to 1000 mL with double-distilled water. The pH value of the buffer solution was then verified on a pH-meter calibrated with three standard buffer solutions. Asp 10 SAC4A and SAC4A assemblies were prepared by dissolving the solids in PBS, and they would self-assemble to form assemblies. CY5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A was prepared by directly mixing PBS solutions of Asp 10 SAC4A and CY5-DM. Q@Asp 10 SAC4A was prepared by mixing the weighed Asp 10 SAC4A and Q solids in a mortar. The mixture was ground for 30 min and dissolved in PBS buffer. D@Asp 10 SAC4A, DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A, Q@SAC4A were prepared in the same way.

Fluorescence titrations were performed in PBS (10 mM, pH = 7.4). The complexations of calix [ 4 ]arenes (Asp 10 SAC4A) with reporter dyes (CY5-DM) were measured by direct fluorescence titrations. A mixed solution containing known amounts of host and guest was sequentially injected into 2.50 mL guest solution in a quartz cuvette. The dye concentrations in mixed solution and cuvette are the same to keep dye concentration constant in the course of titrations. The fluorescence intensity was measured before the first addition and after every addition until a plateau was reached. By fitting the fluorescence intensity according to a 1:1 host-guest binding stoichiometry [ 72 ], the association constant was obtained. The excitation ( λ ex ) and emission ( λ em ) wavelengths of CY5-DM are 635 nm and 654 nm, respectively.

The methodology was based on the solubility variation of the guest molecule (Q or D) with increasing the host molecule (Asp 10 SAC4A or SAC4A) concentration. Briefly, different qualities of PTX solid were mixed with a 1:1 mol ratio of host solid in a mortar, respectively. The mixtures were ground for 30 min and collected with 5 mL PBS in bottles. Then, let them stayed for 6 h and taken the supernatant in other bottles to acquired clear solutions. The supernatants were lyophilized with a lyophilizer. After redissolving by methanol appropriately, each sample was filtered by a 0.22 μm membrane filter, the concentrations of Q (or D) in each group were detected by HPLC according to the standard curve ranging from 2.50 to 80.0 µM. where S 0 is the in intrinsic solubility. For Q, the HPLC equipment was used Alliance 2695 system with UV detection at 374 nm. A column (Symmetry ® C18, 5 μm, 4.6 × 250 mm) was employed. The mobile phase was a mixture of methanol-water (75/25, V / V ) and a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min. The chromatographic experiments were carried out at 37 °C, and the injection volume was 10 µL in all experiments. For D, the same conditions were used except for UV detection at 270 nm.

where W L is the weight of the loaded drug and W drug is the weight of drug fed.

The reduction kinetic of Asp 10 SAC4A was detected by UV-Vis spectroscopy. Excess SDT (5 mM) was injected into 2.50 mL of the host solution (10.0 µM) to monitor the time-dependent absorbance at 420 nm at 37 °C. The release kinetics of complexes was detected by fluorescence spectrometry. Excess SDT (5 mM) was injected into 2.50 mL of the CY5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A complex (10.0/10.0 µM) solution in a quartz cuvette to monitor the time-dependent intensity of CY5-DM at 654 nm at 37 °C.

The experimental protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Radiation Medicine, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (Approval No. IRM/2-IACUC-2406-007). All C57BL/6 wild-type mice were purchased from Beijing Spfbiotech Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Mice were housed as 5 mice per cage and maintained in a 12 h light/dark cycle environment at room temperature (23 °C).

A standardized closed diaphyseal femur fracture model was used to simulate fracture healing. Briefly, mice were anesthetized and the right hind leg was debrided and disinfected, and a longitudinal incision was made on the right anterolateral aspect of the patella along the skin and the soft tissues below to expose the right femur while protecting the tendons and muscles. After that, fine scissors were used to create a transverse fracture, and a mouse intramedullary nail was inserted retrogradely from the intercondylar notch for fixation. The tail of the pin was trimmed and buried below the femoral condyle to protect the motor function of the patellofemoral joint. After confirming that the fracture was complete transverse and not comminuted, the subcutaneous tissue was closed to the skin with 4 − 0 silk suture. Postoperative medications were given to relieve pain. The treatment group mice began to receive the corresponding treatment plan (PBS, Asp₁₀SAC4A, D, Q, DQ, D@Asp₁₀SAC4A, Q@Asp₁₀SAC4A, DQ@Asp₁₀SAC4A, or Q@SAC4A) via tail vein injection after surgery. For in-vivo administration, quercetin was given at 1 mg/kg, and dasatinib was co-formulated in the nanoplatform at a D: Q molar ratio of 1:100.

To quantitatively assess the effect of different treatment groups on the fracture healing process, mice were euthanized and femur samples were collected on the 14th postoperative day. The samples were fixed with 10% neutral formaldehyde solution for 24 h and then subjected to Micro-CT (SkyScan 1276). The scanning parameters were set to a resolution of 18 μm, voltage of 65 kV, and current of 400 µA. Subsequently, the images were reconstructed using NRecon software, and the fracture healing site was analyzed and reconstructed in three dimensions quantitatively using the CTAn software, and the analysis indexes included callus bone volume and callus BV/TV.

To verify the in vivo targeting enrichment ability and hypoxia-responsive release properties of the constructed Asp₁₀SAC4A nanosystems at fracture sites, the fluorescent dye Cy5-DM was chosen for labeling. Cy5-DM was encapsulated in SAC4A or Asp₁₀SAC4A, respectively, and prepared as Cy5-DM@SAC4A (100/200 µM) and Cy5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A (100/200 µM) nano-systems, and served as a control group together with free Cy5-DM (100 µM) as a control group. The different formulations were given by tail vein injection to mice with established femur fracture models. At 1 h, 3 h, 6 h and 12 h after injection, the fluorescence distribution signals in the fracture region were collected in real time under isoflurane anesthesia using a small animal in vivo imaging system (IVIS Lumina, Xenogen Corporation, USA), and the dynamic imaging analysis was performed to evaluate the degree of fluorescence signal enrichment in the fracture region and the duration of the fluorescence signal. To further validate the in vivo targeting, mice were euthanized 12 h after injection, and the fracture side and healthy femur were removed ex vivo for in vitro fluorescence imaging. At the same time, the main organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung and kidney) were taken for tissue distribution analysis. Image acquisition and quantitative fluorescence intensity analysis were done using Living Image 4.2 software.

To evaluate the active recognition ability of the system on bone tissues, in vitro HA binding experiments were supplemented to analyze the binding efficiency of Asp 10 SAC4A with hydroxyapatite particles at different time points (0.5, 1, 2, and 24 h), to further validate its targeting affinity for the surface of neonatal bone mineralization.

Mice were euthanized on the 14th postoperative day, and the femur at the fracture site was collected with intact osteoclastic structures, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 h, and then transferred to 0.5 mol/L EDTA decalcification solution (pH = 8.0) for 7 days. After completion of decalcification, the samples were paraffin-embedded after gradient dehydration with ethanol and transparent treatment with xylene, and sectioned along the long axis of the bone (5 μm in thickness) for hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining and safranin O-fast green staining. After image acquisition, the cartilage area and mature bone tissue area in the bone scab were quantitatively analyzed using ImageJ software.

For immunofluorescence staining, fresh fractured lateral femurs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 4 h, then decalcified in 0.5 mol/L EDTA (pH = 7.4) at 4 °C for 24 h. Subsequently, they were dehydrated with 30% sucrose overnight, embedded in OCT (SAKURA), and sliced longitudinally (15 μm in thickness) and set aside. Sections were washed three times with PBS, treated with 0.3% Triton X-100 for 30 min at room temperature, and then blocked with 5% donkey serum for 1 h. Primary antibodies (as follows) were added and incubated overnight at 4 °C: P16 (Proteintech, 10883-1-AP, 1:100); γ-H2A.X (Zen-bio, 201082-7G9, 1:100); CCL7 (ABclonal, A23288, 1:100). Subsequently PBS was washed 3 times, and the samples were incubated with adapted Alexa Fluor series fluorescent secondary antibody (Proteintech, dilution 1:500) at room temperature for 75 min. Nuclei were re-stained with DAPI, and the final mounting was made using antifade mounting medium (Abkine). All images of tissue sections were acquired by fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan), and quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity and positive area was performed using ImageJ software.

Primary mouse bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) were purchased from Servicebio (Catalog number STCC6011P). The manufacturer certified that these cells were mycoplasma-free. Upon receipt, BMSCs were cultured in specialized complete medium (Servicebio). Cells were seeded into T25 culture flasks and maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO₂. The medium was replaced every 2–3 days. When the confluency reached approximately 80%, cells were passaged using standard trypsinization protocols. BMSCs from passages 2 to 4 were used for all experiments.

Senescent BMSCs were first established by treating the cells with 200 µM hydrogen peroxide for 4 h and incubating them in fresh complete medium for an additional 24 h. Subsequently, senescent BMSCs were transferred to a hypoxic incubator (1% O₂, 5% CO₂, 94% N₂) while being exposed to different drugs. After 24 h of hypoxia treatment, the medium was replaced with osteogenic induction medium. The control group was untreated senescent BMSCs and the treatment group was senescent BMSCs treated with different drugs.

Bone tissue sections and cell samples were stained and analyzed respectively, and the staining was performed according to the instructions of SA-β-Gal Cell Senescence Detection Kit (Beyotime, C0602). Staining of tissue sections: Frozen sections were washed in PBS and placed in the staining solution provided in the kit and incubated in a constant temperature incubator at 37 °C for 12 h (without CO₂). The staining was washed by PBS at the end of staining and photographed microscopically. Positive cells showed blue precipitation, and multiple images of bone callus areas were randomly selected and analyzed for the proportion of positive area using ImageJ software. In vitro cell staining: Cells were washed with PBS and fixed in the fixative provided in the kit for 15 min, washed with PBS and added to the staining working solution, and incubated at 37 °C and protected from light for 12 h. Photographs were taken at the end of the staining and the proportion of positive cells (percentage of blue-stained cells to the total number of cells) was calculated in order to assess the efficiency of senescent cell removal in each treatment group.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) staining and Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining experiments were carried out after the completion of senescence induction and hypoxia culture. ALP staining: BMSCs were stained in 6-well plates 7 days after induction of osteogenic differentiation. Cells were washed with PBS and fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, followed by ALP staining kit (Beyotime, C3206) according to the instructions. The reaction was terminated after incubation with the staining solution for 30 min, washed with PBS and images were taken. The ALP-positive areas were purple in color, representing early osteogenic activity, and the images were analyzed using ImageJ software to calculate the percentage of positive area. ARS: BMSCs were stained with ARS to detect calcified nodule formation after 21 days of osteogenic induction culture. Cells were washed with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, and then stained with 0.2% alizarin red S solution (pH = 4.2, Solarbio, G1452) for 30 min. Excess staining solution was subsequently removed, and photographs were taken for recordings after PBS washing.

Total protein of the samples from each experimental group of fracture tissues and in vitro cells was extracted by RIPA lysate (Beyotime) containing protease inhibitors and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by BCA method (Abkine). Samples were boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and 20 µg protein/sample was separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After membrane closure, primary antibodies were incubated overnight at 4 °C. Primary antibodies used included: P16 (Proteintech, 10883-1-AP, 1:1000); P21 (Proteintech, 10355-1-AP, 1:1000); RUNX2 (Proteintech, 20700-1-AP, 1: 1000); OPN (Proteintech, 20700-1-AP, 1: 1000); and OPN (Proteintech, 20700-1-AP, 1: 1000). 1000); OPN (Proteintech, 22952-1-AP, 1:1000); CCL7 (ABclonal, A23288, 1:1000); β-ACTIN (Proteintech, 20536-1-AP, 1:1000). The membranes were washed by TBST on the following day and the corresponding horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-labeled secondary antibody was added and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized by an enhanced chemiluminescence detection kit (Abkine) and images were acquired under a chemiluminescence imaging system (Tanon). The relative gray values of protein bands were quantified using ImageJ software and normalized with β-ACTIN as an internal reference.

Total RNA of cultured cells was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Scientific) following the manufacturer’s instructions. 1ug of total RNA was then reverse-transcribed into cDNA using All-in-One cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (TransGen Biotech). qRT‒PCR was performed with PerfectStart ® Green qPCR SuperMix (TransGen Biotech) on QuantStudio 3 real-time PCR system (ThermoFisher Scientific). Relative expression was calculated for each gene by the 2 − ΔΔCT method, and GAPDH amplification was used as an internal normalization. Sequences of the primers used for each gene are listed in Supplementary Table S1.

Each experiment was set to three or five groups in parallel, and all data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (s.d.). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s post-test were used to analyze the significant differences in the data for each group. Statistical analysis between two groups was conducted using two-tailed Student’s t-tests. GraphPad Prism software was employed for statistical analysis. Statistical significance was denoted as follows: * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001.
sections.results:
In order to explore the spatial and temporal distribution characteristics of senescent cells in the early stages of fracture healing and their potential pathological roles, we firstly successfully established a mouse femur fracture model and focused on the expression dynamics of p16 Ink4a and p21 Cip1 , important markers related to senescence [ 28 ]. Real-time PCR results showed that the mRNA expression levels of both p16 (Cdkn2a) and p21 (Cdkn1a) peaked at day 14 after fracture, followed by a significant decrease at day 21 (Fig. 1A, B). Further Western blot results were consistent with the mRNA trends: P16 and P21 protein levels increased gradually with the fracture progression, both reaching their peaks at day 14 post-fracture, followed by a significant decrease at day 21 (Fig. 1C-E). These data suggest the existence of a distinct peak period of cellular senescence after fracture injury.

In addition, we further verified the presence and distribution of senescent cells in the fracture region using immunofluorescence staining and senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) staining. γ-H2A.X, as a specific marker for DNA double-strand break damage, is widely used to identify the DNA damage characteristics of senescent cells [ 29 ]. Immunofluorescence analysis showed that P16 and γ-H2A.X were significantly co-localized in the bone callus tissue at day 14 after fracture and were widely present in the region of active healing (Fig. 1F), suggesting that injury-induced cellular senescence is accompanied by significant DNA damage. Further SA-β-Gal staining also confirmed the presence of a large number of typical senescent cells in the fracture region (Fig. 1G).

Taken together, our findings demonstrate that senescent cells emerge rapidly after fracture and accumulate to a distinct peak during the critical early phase of callus formation. Persistent DNA damage and abundant SA-β-Gal positivity further highlight the pathological nature of this senescence response. Senescent cells have been shown to impair tissue repair in multiple contexts and their clearance alleviates age-related pathologies in vivo [ 30 , 31 ]. Therefore, considering the detrimental impact of early senescent cell accumulation on fracture healing, we reasoned that timely elimination of these cells may represent a potential therapeutic strategy.

Base on the observed early and transient accumulation of senescent cells at fracture sites (Fig. 1), we next assessed whether systemic senolytic therapy could improve fracture repair. We used the classical senolytic drug combination of D with Q. Among them, D, as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, induces apoptosis in many types of senescent cells, while Q enhances the clearance effect by interfering with anti-apoptotic pathways, such as Bcl-2, and attenuates SASP levels [ 32 ]. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the combination of D and Q can exhibit synergistic scavenging effects superior to those of single agents in multiple tissues and disease models, with the advantage of both broad-spectrum and selectivity [ 23 , 33 ]. Mice were treated intravenously with the senolytic cocktail dasatinib (D) and quercetin (Q) shortly after fracture, using a dosing strategy of Q = 1 mg/kg and D = 0.1 mg/kg (mass ratio of 1:10). We selected the intravenous route to circumvent the poor oral bioavailability and first-pass metabolism of quercetin [ 34 – 36 ], which severely limit systemic exposure after gavage. Intravenous dosing provides direct systemic availability and generates a transient, pulse-like exposure profile that is particularly suited to senolytics, whose efficacy depends on short-term target engagement rather than sustained drug levels (“hit-and-run” pharmacology) [ 20 , 24 ].

We systematically administered D + Q in a mouse femur fracture model (Fig. 2 A) to evaluate its effect in removing senescent cells and promoting bone healing in vivo. We chose Day 14 for evaluation as it marks the critical inflection point of endochondral ossification and the peak burden of senescent cells, providing the optimal window to assess the efficacy of our Senolytic nanoplatform. SA-β-Gal staining revealed a significant elimination of senescent cells in the D + Q group relative to PBS controls (Fig. 2 B). Consistently, immunofluorescence of P16 and γ-H2A.X demonstrated a decreased proportion of double-positive nuclei (Fig. 2 C), and Western blot results confirmed significant downregulation of the senescence markers P16 and P21 (Fig. 2 D, E). Structural assessments further supported these findings: gross morphology showed increased callus size (Fig. 2 F), while Micro-CT reconstructions and quantitative analysis demonstrated larger callus formation with significantly higher callus volume and bone volume fraction (BV/TV) (Fig. 2 G, H). Finally, histological analyses (HE and Safranin O–fast green staining) revealed enhanced trabecular bone deposition, indicating more advanced fracture tissue remodeling stage in the D + Q-treated group (Fig. 2 I, J).

In conclusion, these results demonstrate that systemic administration of D + Q can effectively attenuate cellular senescence in the fracture callus and promote fracture repair. However, the free-drug approach is constrained by poor solubility, rapid clearance, and non-specific biodistribution [ 36 – 40 ]. Senescent cells in certain tissues contribute to physiological remodeling and homeostasis, and non-targeted senolysis may inadvertently eliminate these beneficial populations, leading to adverse effects [ 24 , 41 – 45 ]. In addition, systemic administration is difficult to achieve effective drug accumulation in the fracture site, which affects the therapeutic efficiency. Although local injection could theoretically increase drug concentration, repeated puncture of fracture sites is not a viable option in clinical practice and would be painful for patients. Moreover, repeated needle punctures may disrupt the fracture hematoma [ 46 , 47 ] and increase the risk of bone infection [ 48 , 49 ]. Many fractures are not directly accessible from the body surface and local injections risk damaging nerves or disrupting the delicate regenerative microenvironment. These limitations underscore the necessity for an advanced delivery system capable of achieving selective accumulation at fracture sites, responding to local hypoxia for on-demand release, and simultaneously enhancing the solubility and ratio-controlled co-delivery of D and Q.

To address the problems of insufficient targeting and significant systemic side effects in the treatment of systemic removal of senescent cells (senolytics), there is an urgent need for the development of novel efficient and controllable drug delivery systems. In recent years, calixarene, as a macrocyclic host molecule with good modification flexibility and excellent biocompatibility, has received much attention in the field of supramolecular drug delivery [ 50 – 52 ]. In particular, macrocyclic-based delivery systems have the unique advantage of “precise ratio loading” and “simultaneous release” of multiple drugs, which is essential for the synergistic effect of senolytics combination [ 53 ]. On this basis, the introduction of an azo group can give the system the ability to respond to the hypoxic environment. Due to the prevailing low-oxygen microenvironment in the fracture region [ 54 , 55 ], the azo structure is reduced and fractured by the highly expressed local azoreductase enzyme, which triggers the local release of the drug and realizes the spatially precise and temporally controllable “smart” controlled release. In addition, the azo modification significantly deepens the molecular cavity of calixarene, which effectively improves the binding affinity of the drug and significantly reduces the risk of non-specific release in the blood circulation [ 25 ]. To achieve active targeting of the fracture site, a sulfhydryl-modified decameric aspartic acid peptide (SH-Asp 10 ) was conjugated to a maleimide-functionalized azocalix [ 4 ]arene (Mal-SAC4A) via a click chemistry reaction. The resulting construct could specifically recognize and bind with high affinity to the surface of freshly exposed HA, thereby enabling efficient drug enrichment at the fracture site (Fig. 3 A; Figure S1 –S5). The superior bone-targeting capability of Asp 10 derivatives is primarily driven by the ionic and coordinative interactions between their carboxyl groups and Ca²⁺ on the bone mineral surface [ 56 – 58 ]. Furthermore, during the early stages of fracture, a substantial amount of ‘freshly exposed’ hydroxyapatite (HA) comes into direct contact with the systemic circulation. In contrast, mature bone surfaces are typically shielded by the periosteum or osteoid barriers. Consequently, the selective affinity of Asp 10 for newly exposed HA facilitates its preferential enrichment at the fracture site rather than in mature bone tissue. Compared with traditional bone-targeting strategies such as bisphosphonates, Asp 10 not only possesses excellent targeting ability, but also significantly reduces the risk of side effects due to its rapid metabolism and short residual time, thus realizing the ideal pharmacokinetic characteristics of “hit-and-run”. In conclusion, a novel supramolecular nanodrug delivery platform, Asp 10 SAC4A, has been successfully designed and synthesized in this study, which provides a new strategy for the realization of efficient and safe senolytics therapy.

The amphiphilic nature of Asp 10 SAC4A enables spontaneous self-assembly into nanostructures in aqueous solution. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) analysis revealed a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 168 ± 5 nm (Figs. 3 B, C). Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) characterisation confirmed these measurements, demonstrating spherical morphology with narrow size distribution and excellent stability. Zeta potential measurements indicated an overall negative surface charge (Fig. 3 D), a property that helps minimise protein adsorption and enhances retention within bone tissue under physiological conditions. Phase solubility diagrams were employed to quantify the association constants ( K a ) between Asp 10 SAC4A and drugs D/Q. Asp 10 SAC4A significantly enhanced aqueous solubility for both drugs, with calculated K a values of (2.93 ± 0.22) × 10 7 M − 1 and (6.62 ± 0.77) × 10 5 M − 1 for D and Q respectively (Figs. 3 E-F). These strong binding affinities ensure effective drug loading capacity. The drug-loaded formulations D@Asp 10 SAC4A, Q@Asp 10 SAC4A and DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A exhibited marginally increased hydrodynamic diameters (179 ± 6 nm, 182 ± 7 nm and 186 ± 7 nm respectively) alongside slight zeta potential reductions compared to unloaded Asp 10 SAC4A (Figs. 3 C, D, S6-S8). SAC4A was selected as control material due to its comparable drug binding affinities (Figures S9-S10) while lacking the bone-targeting moieties present in Asp 10 SAC4A. Drug loading studies demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and drug loading content (DLC) for both D and Q, with controlled ratio loading achievable in the co-loaded formulation (Figure S11). Moreover, DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A maintained excellent colloidal stability over 72 h at 37°C, as reflected by stable particle size and PDI (Figure S17), underscoring its suitability for systemic administration. This establishes a material foundation for personalised ‘tailored’ senolytic combination therapies.

To evaluate the hypoxia-responsive release characteristics of the platform, we systematically monitored the reduction kinetics of Asp 10 SAC4A and associated drug release profiles. Sodium dithionite (SDT) was employed as an in vitro mimic of azoreductase activity, with absorbance at 420 nm tracked using a UV-vis spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies, USA). A rapid decrease in the 420 nm absorption peak of Asp 10 SAC4A over time confirmed cleavage of the azo bond (Fig. 3 G and S12). The absorbance decay followed pseudo first-order kinetics, yielding a reduction half-life of < 1 min for Asp 10 SAC4A (Figure S13). Given that calixarene-dye complexes typically exhibit fluorescence quenching, the fluorescent probe 1,1’,3,3,3’,3’-hexamethylindodicarbocyanine (CY5-DM) was selected as a model drug to precisely monitor release kinetics and in vivo behaviour. Fluorescence titration confirmed comparable binding affinity between Asp 10 SAC4A and CY5-DM to that observed with therapeutic drugs (Figs. 3 H and S15). When SDT was not added, no significant increase in fluorescence was observed. SDT treatment triggered an immediate fluorescence recovery (Fig. 3 I), demonstrating rapid payload release with a release half-life of < 1 min (Figure S13 and S14). These findings collectively validate the hypoxia-selective rapid-release capability of Asp 10 SAC4A. In addition, CY5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A exhibited no significant fluorescence increase in simulated physiological fluid (containing major plasma components), confirming system stability under normoxic conditions and avoidance of non-specific drug leakage (Fig. 3 J).

Together, these results establish that Asp 10 SAC4A provides a rationally designed nanoplatform that enhances drug solubility, enables ratio-controlled co-loading, ensures colloidal stability, and achieves rapid hypoxia-responsive release, thereby directly addressing the major shortcomings of free-drug senolytic therapy.

To evaluate the fracture targeting ability and hypoxia-responsive release properties of Asp 10 SAC4A in vivo, we prepared the fluorescent dye Cy5-DM in different formulations (free Cy5-DM, Cy5-DM@SAC4A, Cy5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A) and injected intravenously into femur fracture model mice. Subsequently, the drug distribution in the fracture region at different time points was dynamically monitored by in vivo fluorescence imaging. The results showed that Cy5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A could achieve fluorescence signal enrichment at the fracture site 1 h after injection and peaked at 3 h, and maintained a signal after 12 h, which was significantly better than that of the nontargeted Cy5-DM and Cy5-DM@SAC4A groups (Fig. 4 A, B). The fracture hematoma and early callus are characterized by a transient hypoxic microenvironment, accompanied by activation of the HIF-1α signaling pathway, as demonstrated in multiple studies on bone repair [ 59 – 61 ]. Further analysis revealed that Cy5-DM@SAC4A exhibited stronger fracture site signal compared with free Cy5-DM, suggesting that the hypoxia response mechanism contributes to improved local enrichment at the fracture site; whereas Cy5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A further enhanced the enrichment effect on this basis, suggesting that active targeted modification plays a key role in fracture localization. This result suggests that Asp 10 SAC4A has good in vivo stability with active targeting enrichment at the fracture site and can realize intelligent controlled release of drugs in the hypoxic microenvironment of fracture breaks. Further dissection of the fracture site and normal femur for ex vivo fluorescence analysis revealed that the fluorescence intensity of Cy5-DM@Asp 10 SAC4A in fractured femur was significantly higher than that in normal femur and significantly better than that of Cy5-DM with the nontargeted SAC4A delivery system (Fig. 4 C, D). This result further supports the highly selective enrichment ability of Asp 10 SAC4A for the fracture region.

In addition, biodistribution analysis of major organs showed predominant renal accumulation (Fig. 4 E, F), consistent with the renal clearance pathway of Cy5 fluorophores. To mechanistically validate the targeting mechanism, we performed an in vitro hydroxyapatite (HA) binding assay, which demonstrated sustained and significantly stronger binding of Asp 10 SAC4A to HA compared with SAC4A (Fig. 4 G). These findings support that fracture-site enrichment arises from the Asp₁₀–HA interaction. Taken together, the results suggest that the Asp 10 SAC4A nano-delivery system can achieve active targeting enrichment of fracture regions in vivo with excellent stability and hypoxia-responsive release properties.

Although the combination of D and Q has been validated as a senolytic strategy in fracture tissues, previous studies have also emphasized that their efficacy and selectivity depend strongly on the drug ratio due to their distinct and partially non-overlapping mechanisms of pathway [ 32 ]. To identify an optimal ratio for subsequent nanoformulations, we performed combination index (CI) analysis using the Chou–Talalay method across a matrix of D: Q molar ratios and dose levels [ 62 ]. The resulting heatmap (Fig. 5 A) revealed a broad synergy plateau (CI < 1), with the strongest synergy occurring at approximately 1:100 (molar). We next examined whether the Asp 10 SAC4A nanoplatform could deliver D + Q in a manner that is biocompatible under normoxia yet senolytic under hypoxia, recapitulating the fracture microenvironment. Viability assays demonstrated that normal BMSCs maintained high survival across all formulations, confirming the low intrinsic cytotoxicity of the carrier system (Fig. 5 B, left). By contrast, in senescent BMSCs subjected to hypoxic conditions, DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A elicited a significant reduction in viability, outperforming free drugs and the non-targeted formulation (Fig. 5 B, right). Notably, under normoxic conditions this hypoxia-triggered clearance was minimal, underscoring the on-demand release behavior of the system. Collectively, these findings confirm that the Asp 10 SAC4A nanoplatform maintains sufficient biosafety in physiological environments, while activating potent senolysis specifically under hypoxia. This nanoplatform directly addresses the requirement for microenvironment-specific senolytic engagement during fracture repair.

To further corroborate the senolytic capacity of the nanoplatform, we assessed hallmark markers of cellular senescence under hypoxic conditions, using dasatinib at 200 nM and quercetin at 20 µM, corresponding to the optimized 1:100 molar ratio. SA-β-Gal staining revealed a substantial reduction of senescent cells following treatment with drug-loaded nanoformulations, with significantly greater clearance than that observed in the free drug-treated group (Fig. 5 C). Consistently, Western blot results demonstrated significant downregulation of P16 and P21 in senescent BMSCs exposed to drug-loaded nanoformulations compared with free drugs or empty carriers (Fig. 5 D–F). In addition, the scavenging ability of the drug-loaded nanoplatforms was significantly weakened under normoxic conditions, suggesting that the system has a good hypoxic responsiveness. These results reinforce the conclusion that the nanoplatform exerts selective and efficient clearance of senescent cells in a hypoxia-dependent manner, in agreement with the viability assays (Fig. 5 B).

Given that senescence imposes a profound inhibitory effect on mesenchymal osteogenic differentiation [ 63 , 64 ], we next examined whether hypoxia-activated senolysis by the nanoplatform could restore osteogenic potential. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) staining and Alizarin Red S (ARS) assays demonstrated enhanced ALP activity and increased calcium nodule formation in the drug-loaded group relative to controls, predominantly under hypoxia (Fig. 5 G). At the molecular level, expression of osteogenic transcription factors was significantly improved, with RUNX2 and OPN upregulated in drug-loaded groups compared with free drugs and carriers (Fig. 5 H–J). These findings indicate that the removal of senescent cells by the optimized nanoplatform directly contributes to the rescue of osteogenic function in senescent BMSCs.

Under in-vitro culture conditions, the presence of the Asp₁₀ peptide did not confer additional advantage over the non-targeted SAC4A carrier, as no exposed hydroxyapatite interface is available for active binding. Thus, Asp 10 SAC4A and SAC4A exhibited comparable senolytic and pro-osteogenic activity in vitro. This outcome is consistent with the design principle of the platform: Asp 10 is expected to exert its contribution only in vivo, where freshly mineralized bone surfaces become exposed at fracture sites. In conclusion, although the bone-targeting properties of Asp 10 could not be reflected in vitro, the drug-carrying nanoplatform constructed in this study exhibited good drug containment under normoxic conditions. It was able to significantly promote senescent cell clearance and osteogenic differentiation in a simulated fracture hypoxic microenvironment through enhanced drug solubility and precise hypoxia-responsive release. This in vitro validation demonstrates that the platform has excellent microenvironment-specific response characteristics and is capable of realizing specific microenvironmental precision anti-senescence therapy, avoiding the non-specific removal of beneficial senescent cells in the conventional physiological state.

To further clarify the fracture-targeted senescent cell removal effect and the ability to promote fracture healing of the Asp 10 SAC4A-loaded nanoplatform in vivo, we utilized a mouse femur fracture model and compared nine treatment groups, including vehicle, free drugs, single-drug nanoformulations, a non-targeted formulation, and the targeted dual-drug nanoplatform, with analyses performed on day 14 post-fracture (Fig. 6 A).

Histological and molecular analyses consistently demonstrated that DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A (D: Q molar ratio 1:100) most effectively reduced the senescent cell burden within fracture callus. SA-β-Gal staining revealed a markedly smaller senescence-positive fraction in this group compared with free DQ, single-drug nanoformulations, or non-targeted carriers (Fig. 6 B, C). Western blot results further substantiated these findings, showing downregulation of P16 and P21 (Fig. 6 D, E). These results establish that targeted co-delivery confers more efficient senolysis in vivo than systemic administration of free drugs.

The reduction of senescence burden was accompanied by accelerated fracture structural regeneration. Gross observation revealed enlarged callus formation in the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A group (Fig. 6 F), and Micro-CT reconstructions demonstrated significant increases in callus volume and BV/TV relative to all controls (Fig. 6 G, H). Further quantitative analysis by Micro-CT of callus showed that DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A significantly outperformed both free DQ and the single-drug nanoplatforms ( p < 0.05), highlighting that targeted ratio-controlled co-delivery confers therapeutic superiority beyond either free or single-agent delivery. Histological evaluation further substantiated these findings. Safranin O–fast green and HE staining demonstrated accelerated cartilage clearance and extensive trabecular bone deposition in the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A group, with quantification confirming a markedly lower cartilaginous fraction relative to all other groups (Fig. 6 I–K). These results are indicative of accelerated endochondral ossification and advanced callus maturation.

The above results clearly indicate that the Asp 10 SAC4A fracture-targeted nano-delivery strategy was able to significantly enhance senescent cell clearance in vivo, which is highly consistent with the results of the previous in vivo enrichment experiment (Fig. 4 ). It is worth mentioning that although the advantage of Asp 10 -targeted modification was not revealed under in vitro experimental conditions, this bone-targeting effect contributed significantly to the therapeutic effect in the actual fracture microenvironment (in vivo conditions). This suggests that the ability of the Asp 10 moiety to bind specifically to the fracture tissue effectively increased the senolytic local drug concentration and senescent cell clearance efficiency under in vivo conditions, thereby significantly improving the local microenvironment of fracture healing. Furthermore, the tissue staining of the major organs in mice indicated that different groups exhibited no potential in vivo toxicity (Figure S16). Although biodistribution analysis indicated predominant renal clearance of the formulation (Fig. 4 ), no pathological lesions were observed in the kidneys, suggesting that renal accumulation did not elicit overt toxicity within the study period.

In summary, the results of the in vivo experiments confirmed that the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A nanoplatform significantly accelerated the fracture repair process through the synergistic effects of proportional delivery, precise fracture-targeted enrichment, hypoxia-corresponding controlled release, and enhanced drug solubility. This provides important experimental evidence for subsequent clinical translational applications and further emphasizes the great potential of precision fracture-targeted anti-senescence strategy in fracture therapy.

To further explore the potential mechanism by which the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A platform significantly improves fracture healing, we further examined the expression levels of SASP factors in tissues of the fracture region. The SASP factors play a key role in the local accumulation of senescent cells, which can deteriorate the local microenvironment through the secretion of large amounts of inflammatory chemokines and cytokines, thus hindering the repair and regeneration process of fractures [ 65 ].

First, we analyzed the overall expression differences of SASP-associated inflammatory factors and chemokines between the fracture region and normal tissues by heatmap, and the results showed that the expression levels of several pro-inflammatory factors and chemokines (especially CCL7, IL-6, CXCL1, etc.) were significantly upregulated in the fracture region (Fig. 7 A). In particular, the chemokine CCL7 was significantly highly expressed in the fracture tissues, which was highly consistent with the important role of CCL7 in the bone inflammatory microenvironment proposed in recent studies [ 66 – 68 ].

Therapeutic intervention with DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A significantly attenuated this aberrant inflammatory response. Immunofluorescence staining of CCL7 demonstrated markedly reduced signal intensity in callus from the targeted dual-drug group compared with PBS controls (Fig. 7 B). Subsequently, we examined the mRNA expression level of CCL7 in the fracture site tissues using qRT-PCR, and found that the expression of CCL7 within the fracture tissues of the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A treatment group was significantly lower than that of the PBS group (Fig. 7 C), suggesting that this delivery platform significantly suppressed the aberrant expression of chemokines in the fracture microenvironment. Further Western blot results also verified this trend: the expression levels of CCL7, P16, and P21 proteins were significantly lower in the fracture tissues of the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A group (Fig. 7 D, E), further suggesting that it reduces the senescence-associated SASP secretion effect by selectively removing senescent cells.

Based on the above experimental results, we found that the DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A nanoplatform plays a major role in promoting fracture healing by removing senescent cells from the fracture microenvironment. The removal of senescent cells effectively reduced the secretion of local SASP factors, which further alleviated the inflammatory response and optimized the tissue repair microenvironment. This mechanistic cascade of action provides theoretical and experimental basis for significantly enhancing the effectiveness of fracture treatment, and further highlights the importance of precise removal of senescent cells in the field of fracture treatment.

sections.conclusion:
In this study, we found that senescent cells rapidly accumulate at fracture sites following injury, and their continuous secretion of SASP factors significantly exacerbates the local inflammation and disrupts the regenerative microenvironment, thus becoming an important factor hindering fracture healing. Removal of senescent cells can break the negative loop and significantly accelerate fracture repair. Despite the demonstrated efficacy of traditional senolytic drugs, their clinical application still faces three major challenges: insufficient precision in senescent cell clearance, lack of local microenvironment-responsive release capability, and limited multidrug synergistic delivery.

To address these challenges, we successfully designed and synthesized a supramolecular nanoplatform based on an Asp 10 -modified azo macrocycle (Asp 10 SAC4A). Firstly, the carrier realized the precise targeting enrichment of drugs to the fracture region by the introduction of Asp 10 peptide; secondly, the introduction of azo bond structure in the platform provides a sensitive response to the hypoxic environment, which enables the drug to be released at the fracture site in a controlled spatio-temporal manner on demand, thus maximizing the efficiency and safety of the local treatment; thirdly, the cavity structure of SAC4A macrocycle significantly enhanced the water solubility of hydrophobic drugs D and Q, and realized stable fixed-ratio co-loading, which guaranteed the synergistic effect of the coupled drugs. The DQ@Asp 10 SAC4A platform achieves high efficiency in senescent cell clearance, significantly reduces the expression level of SASP factors (e.g., CCL7), inhibits inflammatory cascade, breaks the negative microenvironmental cycle, and ultimately accelerates the repair of bone tissue. The theoretical basis and therapeutic targets of its treatment were elucidated. Unlike previous studies that primarily focused on systemic senolytic administration, our work emphasizes a precision anti-senescence strategy by simultaneously achieving lesion-specific targeting, microenvironment-triggered activation, and ratio-controlled combination therapy in fracture healing. In conclusion, this study presents a precise anti-senescence therapeutic strategy based on fracture targeting and hypoxia response. Our findings indicate that this strategy can reduce the local senescence burden and improve the fracture microenvironment in mice, providing a proof-of-concept for precision anti-senescence interventions in bone tissue engineering. However, important challenges remain for clinical translation. Future studies should focus on further optimizing the delivery system, validating efficacy in diverse and clinically relevant models, and systematically evaluating long-term safety and effectiveness to support the translational potential of this emerging therapeutic approach.
